cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: Ed, how are you getting on with the reading for our presentation next week?

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: I know, I hadn't realised birth order was such a popular area of research.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: But the stuff on birth order and personality is mostly unreliable.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: From what I've been reading a lot of claims about how your position in the family

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: determines certain personality traits are just stereotypes, with no robust evidence to

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: support them.

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: OK, but that's an interesting point – we could start by outlining what previous research

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: has shown. There are studies going back over a hundred years.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: Yeah – so we could just run through some of the typical traits.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: Like the consensus seems to be that oldest children are generally less well-adjusted

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: because they never get over the arrival of a younger sibling.

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: Right, but on a positive note, some studies claimed that they were thought to be good a

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: nurturing – certainly in the past when people had large families they would have been

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: expected to look after the younger ones.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: There isn't such a clear picture for middle children – but one trait that a lot of the

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: studies mention is that they are easier to get on with than older or younger siblings.

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: Generally eager to please and helpful – although that's certainly not accurate as far as

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: my family goes – my middle brother was a nightmare – always causing fights and envious of

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: whatever I had.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: As I said – none of this seems to relate to my own experience.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: I'm the youngest in my family and I don't recognise myself in any of the studies I've

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: read about.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: I'm supposed to have been a sociable and confident child who made friends easily – but I

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: was actually terribly shy.

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: Really? That's funny.

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: There have been hundreds of studies on twins but mostly about nurture versus nature...

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: There was one on personality, which said that a twin is likely to be quite shy in social

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: situations because they always have their twin around to depend on for support.

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: My cousins were like that when they were small – they were only interested in each other

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: and found it hard to engage with other kids. They're fine now though.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: Only children have had a really bad press – a lot of studies have branded them as loners

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: who think the world revolves around them because they've never had to fight for their

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: parents' attention.

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: That does seem a bit harsh.

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: One category I hadn't considered before was children with much older siblings – a couple

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: of studies mentioned that these children grow up more quickly and are expected to do

cues.speaker: TH
cues.text: basic things for themselves – like getting dressed.

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: I can see how that might be true – although I expect they're sometimes the exact opposite

cues.speaker: ED
cues.text: – playing the baby role and clamouring for special treatment.
